This activity reviews the pathophysiology of DM and highlights the role of the interprofessional team in its management. Objectives: * Describe the etiologies of diabetes mellitus. * Review the pathophysiology of diabetes mellitus. * Summarize the treatment options for diabetes mellitus. * Review the importance of improving care coordination among interprofessional team members to improve outcomes for patients affected by diabetes mellitus type 2. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic. Introduction Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by persistent hyperglycemia. It may be due to impaired insulin secretion, resistance to peripheral actions of insulin, or both. According to the International Diabetes Federation (IDF), approximately 415 million adults between the ages of 20 to 79 years had diabetes mellitus in 2015.[1] DM is proving to be a global public health burden as this number is expected to rise to another 200 million by 2040.[1] Chronic hyperglycemia in synergy with the other metabolic aberrations in patients with diabetes mellitus can cause damage to various organ systems, leading to the development of disabling and life-threatening health complications, most prominent of which are microvascular (retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy) and macrovascular complications leading to a 2-fold to 4-fold increased risk of cardiovascular diseases. In this review, we provide an overview of the pathogenesis, diagnosis, clinical presentation, and principles of management of diabetes. Etiology DM is broadly classified into three types by etiology and clinical presentation, type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, and gestational diabetes (GDM). Some other less common types of diabetes include monogenic diabetes and secondary diabetes.[2][3][4][5] Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) accounts for 5% to 10% of DM and is characterized by autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing beta cells in the islets of the pancreas. As a result, there is an absolute deficiency of insulin. A combination of genetic susceptivity and environmental factors such as viral infection, toxins, or some dietary factors have been implicated as triggers for autoimmunity. T1DM is most commonly seen in children and adolescents though it can develop at any age. Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) accounts for around 90% of all cases of diabetes. In T2DM, the response to insulin is diminished, and this is defined as insulin resistance. During this state, insulin is ineffective and is initially countered by an increase in insulin production to maintain glucose homeostasis, but over time, insulin production decreases, resulting in T2DM. T2DM is most commonly seen in persons older than 45 years. Still, it is increasingly seen in children, adolescents, and younger adults due to rising levels of obesity, physical inactivity, and energy-dense diets. Gestational Diabetes Mellitus Hyperglycaemia, which is first detected during pregnancy, is classified as gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), also known as hyperglycemia in pregnancy. Although it can occur anytime during pregnancy, GDM generally affects pregnant women during the second and third trimesters. According to the American Diabetes Association (ADA), GDM complicates 7% of all pregnancies. Women with GDM and their offspring have an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes mellitus in the future. GDM can be complicated by hypertension, preeclampsia, and hydramnios and may also lead to increased operative interventions. The fetus can have increased weight and size (macrosomia) or congenital anomalies. Even after birth, such infants may have respiratory distress syndrome and subsequent childhood and adolescent obesity. Older age, obesity, excessive gestational weight gain, history of congenital anomalies in previous children, or stillbirth, or a family history of diabetes are risk factors for GDM. Monogenic Diabetes A single genetic mutation in an autosomal dominant gene causes this type of diabetes. Examples of monogenic diabetes include conditions like neonatal diabetes mellitus and maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY). Around 1 to 5% of all diabetes cases are due to monogenic diabetes. MODY is a familial disorder and usually presents under the age of 25 years. Secondary Diabetes Secondary diabetes is caused due to the complication of other diseases affecting the pancreas (for example, pancreatitis), hormone disturbances (for example, Cushing disease), or drugs (for example, corticosteroids). fetched_contents.text: Diabetes Diagnosis & Tests There are several ways to diagnose diabetes. Each way usually needs to be repeated on a second day to diagnose diabetes. Testing should be carried out in a health care setting (such as your doctor’s office or a lab). If your doctor determines that your blood glucose (blood sugar) level is very high, or if you have classic symptoms of high blood glucose in addition to one positive test, your doctor may not require a second test to diagnose diabetes. A1C Image The A1C test measures your average blood glucose for the past two to three months. The advantages of being diagnosed this way are that you don't have to fast or drink anything. Diabetes is diagnosed at an A1C of greater than or equal to 6.5% Result A1C Normal less than 5.7% Prediabetes 5.7% to 6.4% Diabetes 6.5% or higher Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Image This test checks your fasting blood glucose levels. Fasting means after not having anything to eat or drink (except water) for at least 8 hours before the test. This test is usually done first thing in the morning, before breakfast. Diabetes is diagnosed at fasting blood glucose of greater than or equal to 126 mg/dl Result Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Normal less than 100 mg/dL Prediabetes 100 mg/dl to 125 mg/dL Diabetes 126 mg/dL or higher Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) Image The OGTT is a two-hour test that checks your blood glucose levels before and two hours after you drink a special sweet drink. It tells the doctor how your body processes sugar. Diabetes is diagnosed at two-hour blood glucose of greater than or equal to 200 mg/dl Result Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) Normal less than 140 mg/dL Prediabetes 140 to 199 mg/dL Diabetes 200 mg/dL or higher Random (also called Casual) Plasma Glucose Test This test is a blood check at any time of the day when you have severe diabetes symptoms. Diabetes is diagnosed at blood glucose of greater than or equal to 200 mg/dl What is Prediabetes? Before people develop type 2 diabetes, they almost always have prediabetes—blood glucose levels that are higher than normal but not yet high enough to be diagnosed as diabetes. Doctors sometimes refer to prediabetes as impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) or impaired fasting glucose (IFG), depending on what test was used when it was detected. This condition puts you at a higher risk for developing type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Symptoms There are no clear symptoms of prediabetes, so you may have it and not know it. Some people with prediabetes may have some of the symptoms of diabetes or even problems from diabetes already. You usually find out that you have prediabetes when being tested for diabetes. If you have prediabetes, you should be checked for type 2 diabetes every one to two years. Results indicating prediabetes are: * An A1C of 5.7–6.4% * Fasting blood glucose of 100–125 mg/dL * An OGTT two-hour blood glucose of 140–199 mg/dL Preventing Type 2 Diabetes You will not develop type 2 diabetes automatically if you have prediabetes. For some people with prediabetes, early treatment can actually return blood glucose levels to the normal range. Research shows that you can lower your risk for type 2 diabetes by 58% by: * Losing 7% of your body weight (or 15 pounds if you weigh 200 pounds) * Exercising moderately (such as brisk walking) 30 minutes a day, five days a week Don't worry if you can't get to your ideal body weight. Losing even 10 to 15 pounds can make a huge difference.

fetched_contents.text: What Are My Options for Type 2 Diabetes Medications? People with type 2 diabetes can use various medications other than insulin to help manage their diabetes effectively. However, individuals with type 1 diabetes must rely on insulin for blood glucose (blood sugar) management. Many type 2 diabetes medications, including oral and injectable options, work in different ways to regulate blood glucose levels. Managing type 2 diabetes involves a comprehensive approach that includes meal planning, regular physical activity, and the right diabetes medications. By combining these three strategies, individuals can effectively regulate their blood glucose levels. Oral medications for type 2 diabetes are commonly prescribed as part of a treatment plan to help maintain stable blood glucose levels. Diabetes is a progressive disease and medications sometimes stop working as well over time. When this happens adjustments to your medication or combination therapy can help, which may include adding insulin to your treatment plan. This doesn't mean you're doing something wrong. Even if diabetes other medications do bring your blood glucose levels near the normal range, you may need to take insulin if you have a severe infection or need surgery. Other medications may not be able to keep your blood glucose levels in your target range during these stressful times that affect your blood glucose. There are different types, or classes, of medications that work in different ways to lower blood glucose levels. Some options are taken by mouth and others are injected. Some of the commonly used classes of non-insulin medications include: * Metformin * Dipeptidyl peptidase 4 (DPP-4) inhibitors * Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) and dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and GLP-1 receptor agonists * Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors * Sulfonylureas * Thiazolidinediones (TZDs) Metformin Metformin (Glucophage) is classified as a biguanide medication and is the only available medication in this class. Metformin lowers blood glucose levels primarily by decreasing the amount of glucose produced by the liver. Metformin also helps lower blood glucose levels by making muscle tissue more sensitive to insulin so blood glucose can be used for energy. It is usually taken two times a day. A side effect of metformin may be diarrhea, but this is improved when the drug is taken with food. DPP-4 Inhibitors DPP-4 inhibitors help improve A1C (a measure of average blood glucose levels over two to three months) without causing hypoglycemia (low blood glucose). They work by preventing the breakdown of naturally occurring hormones in the body, GLP-1 and GIP. These hormones reduce blood glucose levels in the body, but they are broken down very quickly so it does not work well when injected as a drug itself. By interfering in the process that breaks down GLP-1 and GIP, DPP-4 inhibitors allow these hormones to remain active in the body longer, lowering blood glucose levels only when they are elevated. DPP-4 inhibitors do not cause weight gain and are usually very well tolerated. There are four DPP-4 inhibitors currently on the market in the U.S.: * Alogliptin (Nesina) * Linagliptin (Tradjenta) * Saxagliptin (Onglyza) * Sitagliptin (Januvia) GLP-1 and Dual GLP-1/GIP Receptor Agonists As noted in the description for DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 and GIP are natural hormones in the body that help maintain glucose levels. Use of GLP-1 and dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists is another strategy to help use these hormones to improve blood glucose management in people with type 2 diabetes. These medications have similar effects to the GLP-1 and GIP produced in the body but are resistant to being broken down by the DPP-4 enzyme. These medications can result in large benefits on lowering blood glucose and body weight. Some agents in this class have also been shown to prevent heart disease. Most of these medications are injected, with the exception of one that is taken by mouth once daily, called semaglutide (Rybelsus). Injectable GLP-1 receptor agonists currently on the market include: * Dulaglutide (Trulicity) * Exenatide (Byetta) * Exenatide extended-release (Bydureon) * Liraglutide (Victoza) * Lixisenatide (Adlyxin) * Injectable semaglutide (Ozempic) One dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist is currently on the market called tirzepatide (Mounjaro). How often you need to inject these medications varies from twice daily to once weekly, depending on the medication. The most common side effect with these medications is nausea and vomiting, which is more common when starting or increasing the dose. SGLT2 Inhibitors Glucose in the bloodstream passes through the kidneys where it can either be excreted in the urine or reabsorbed back into the blood. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) works in the kidney to reabsorb glucose. A new class of medication, SGLT2 inhibitors, block this action, causing excess glucose to be eliminated in the urine. By increasing the amount of glucose excreted in the urine, people can see improved blood glucose, some weight loss, and small decreases in blood pressure. ## What blood tests and criteria are used to diagnose type 2 diabetes?

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using blood tests that measure glucose or average glucose over time. The main tests are:

- **A1C test**: Measures average blood glucose over the past 2 to 3 months. An A1C of **6.5% or higher** confirms diabetes [N2-F2].  
- **Fasting plasma glucose (FPG)**: Measures glucose after at least 8 hours of fasting. A fasting blood glucose of **126 mg/dL or higher** confirms diabetes [N2-F2].  
- **Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)**: Measures glucose before and 2 hours after drinking a sweet drink. A 2-hour blood glucose of **200 mg/dL or higher** confirms diabetes [N2-F2].  
- **Random blood glucose test**: Measures glucose at any time. A random blood glucose of **200 mg/dL or higher**, especially with symptoms of high blood sugar, may confirm diabetes [N2-F2].  

Prediabetes is the intermediate stage before diabetes and is diagnosed with:
- A1C of **5.7% to 6.4%**
- Fasting blood glucose of **100 to 125 mg/dL**
- OGTT 2-hour blood glucose of **140 to 199 mg/dL** [N2-F2].

## Common symptoms and signs that may point to the condition

Type 2 diabetes often has no clear symptoms at first, but people may notice:
- **Frequent urination** [N6-R3]
- **Excessive thirst** [N6-R5]
- **High blood glucose levels** [N6-R3]
- **High levels of ketones in the urine** [N6-R3]
- **Weight loss**, even if the person is overweight [N6-R5]
- **Blurred vision** [N6-R5]
- **Fatigue** or **weakness** [N6-R5]
- **Dry skin and mouth** [N6-R2]
- **Flushing face** or **muscle stiffness or aches** [N6-R2]

These signs are not exclusive to diabetes and can overlap with other conditions, so testing is needed for confirmation [N2-F2].

## Differences between prediabetes, diabetes, and other related conditions

- **Prediabetes**: Blood glucose levels are higher than normal but not high enough to be diagnosed as diabetes. It is a warning sign and can be reversed with lifestyle changes [N2-F2].
- **Diabetes**: Blood glucose levels are high enough to cause symptoms and meet one of the diagnostic criteria listed above [N2-F2].
- **Other related conditions**:
  - **Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)**: A severe, life-threatening complication of diabetes where the body produces high levels of ketones and blood glucose is extremely high. It is not the same as prediabetes or ordinary diabetes, and it requires urgent care [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].
  - **Hyperglycemia**: High blood glucose that may be part of diabetes, prediabetes, or other disorders [N6-R5].
  - **Hypoglycemia**: Low blood glucose, which is not the same as diabetes but can occur with insulin or certain medications [N6-R4].

The distinction matters because prediabetes is treatable, diabetes needs ongoing management, and DKA is a medical emergency [N2-F2][N6-R3].

## Major complications and how they develop over time

Type 2 diabetes can damage organs and blood vessels over time, leading to complications:

- **Heart disease and stroke**: Persistent high blood sugar damages blood vessels and the heart, increasing the risk of heart attack, stroke, and cardiovascular disease [N4-R1][N4-R5].
- **Kidney disease**: Diabetes can damage the kidneys, leading to chronic kidney disease. This can worsen over time and may eventually require dialysis or transplant [N4-R3][N4-R4].
- **Nerve damage (neuropathy)**: High blood sugar injures nerves, especially in the feet and hands, causing pain, numbness, or weakness [N4-R3][N4-R4].
- **Eye problems**: Diabetes damages blood vessels in the retina, increasing the risk of retinopathy, cataracts, and glaucoma [N4-R4].
- **Foot problems**: Nerve damage and poor circulation can lead to ulcers, infections, and, in severe cases, amputation [N4-R3].
- **Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)**: A severe complication where the body produces high levels of ketones and blood glucose is extremely high. DKA can develop rapidly and is a medical emergency [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

These complications develop gradually because high blood sugar harms blood vessels and organs over years, especially if blood glucose is not well controlled [N4-R4][N4-R5].

## Steps to reduce risk of heart disease, kidney disease, and nerve damage

The best way to reduce risk is to keep blood glucose, blood pressure, and cholesterol within target ranges. Evidence-based steps include:

- **Controlling blood glucose** with medication, diet, and lifestyle changes [N3-F3].
- **Managing blood pressure**: High blood pressure worsens diabetes complications, so it should be kept below target [N4-R1][N4-R4].
- **Lowering cholesterol**: Especially LDL cholesterol, to reduce heart disease risk [N4-R1][N4-R5].
- **Losing weight and keeping weight stable**: Weight loss improves insulin sensitivity and reduces complications [N3-F3][N5-F4].
- **Physical activity**: Exercise improves blood glucose control, lowers cardiovascular risk, and improves well-being [N5-R1][N5-R3].
- **Smoking cessation**: Smoking increases heart disease and other complications [N5-F4].
- **Checking feet regularly**: For nerve damage and ulcers [N4-R3].
- **Controlling other risk factors**: Such as sleep apnea, obesity, and inflammation [N4-R4].

## Screening recommendations and early intervention signals

Early detection and intervention are key. Recommended screenings include:

- **Annual A1C testing** to monitor average blood glucose [N2-F2].
- **Annual eye exams** to detect retinopathy early [N4-R4].
- **Kidney function tests**, including urine albumin and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), to detect kidney disease early [N4-R3].
- **Foot exams** for neuropathy, ulcers, and poor circulation [N4-R3].
- **Cardiovascular risk assessment**, including blood pressure and cholesterol checks [N4-R1][N4-R5].

Early intervention signals include:
- **High blood glucose levels**
- **Ketones in the urine**
- **Blurred vision**
- **Excessive thirst or frequent urination**
- **Foot pain, numbness, or sores**
- **Swelling in the legs or feet**
- **Changes in vision or eye pain**

If any of these signals appear, the patient should contact a healthcare provider promptly [N2-F2][N6-R3][N4-R3].

## First-line and second-line treatment options including lifestyle changes

The treatment approach for type 2 diabetes is usually **lifestyle first**, followed by **medications** if needed.

### First-line treatment
- **Lifestyle changes** are the foundation of management. These include:
  - **Diet**: Eating balanced meals with appropriate carbohydrates, protein, and healthy fats [N5-F4].
  - **Exercise**: At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week, plus strength training [N5-F4].
  - **Weight loss**: Losing even a small amount of weight can improve blood glucose control [N5-F4].
- **Metformin** is the most commonly prescribed first-line medication because it is effective, safe, and generally does not cause hypoglycemia [N3-F3][N7-R3].

### Second-line and other treatment options
If metformin alone is not enough, additional medications may be added:
- **DPP-4 inhibitors** (e.g., sitagliptin, saxagliptin) help improve A1C by increasing active GLP-1 and GIP hormones [N3-F3].
- **GLP-1 receptor agonists** (e.g., dulaglutide, liraglutide, semaglutide) are injectable medications that improve glucose control and may also help with weight loss [N3-F3][N3-R2].
- **SGLT2 inhibitors** (e.g., empagliflozin, canagliflozin) lower glucose by excreting excess glucose in the urine and may reduce heart and kidney risks [N3-F3].
- **Sulfonylureas** stimulate insulin release from the pancreas, but they can cause hypoglycemia [N3-F3].
- **Thiazolidinediones (TZDs)** improve insulin sensitivity but are less commonly used today [N3-F3].

### When to consider insulin
Insulin is usually added when blood glucose is not well controlled with other medications, especially during illness, surgery, or severe stress [N3-F3].

## How different medications work and their side effects

- **Metformin**:
  - Works by reducing glucose production in the liver and improving insulin sensitivity in muscle tissue [N3-F3].
  - Common side effect: diarrhea, which often improves when taken with food [N3-F3].

- **DPP-4 inhibitors**:
  - Prevent the breakdown of GLP-1 and GIP, allowing these hormones to lower blood glucose when elevated [N3-F3].
  - Side effects are generally mild and do not usually cause weight gain or hypoglycemia [N3-F3].

- **GLP-1 receptor agonists**:
  - Act like natural GLP-1 and GIP hormones; they also reduce appetite and can promote weight loss [N3-F3][N3-R2].
  - Common side effect: nausea and vomiting, especially when starting or increasing the dose [N3-F3].

- **SGLT2 inhibitors**:
  - Block glucose reabsorption in the kidneys, causing glucose to be excreted in the urine [N3-F3].
  - Common side effects include genital yeast infections and urinary tract infections [N3-F3].

- **Sulfonylureas**:
  - Stimulate the pancreas to release more insulin [N3-F3].
  - Can cause hypoglycemia, especially in older adults or those with kidney disease [N3-F3].

## Daily self-management strategies for blood glucose monitoring and diet

A practical daily routine includes:

### Blood glucose monitoring
- Check blood glucose regularly as recommended by the healthcare provider.
- Use self-monitoring devices to track patterns and adjust treatment as needed [N5-F4].
- Check before and after exercise, as physical activity can lower blood glucose [N5-F4].

### Diet
- Eat a balanced diet with a focus on whole foods, fiber, lean protein, and healthy fats [N5-F4].
- Avoid excessive refined sugars, processed foods, and sugary drinks [N5-F4].
- Control portion sizes and manage carbohydrate intake to avoid blood glucose spikes [N5-F4].

### Lifestyle
- **Exercise regularly**: Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week, plus strength training [N5-F4].
- **Stay hydrated**: Drinking enough water helps manage blood glucose and prevents dehydration [N5-F4].
- **Manage stress**: Chronic stress can affect blood glucose and overall health [N5-F4].
- **Sleep well**: Poor sleep can worsen blood glucose control [N5-F4].

### Daily reminders
- Keep a diabetes management journal to record blood glucose readings, meals, exercise, and symptoms [N5-F4].
- Check with the healthcare provider before starting any new exercise, medication, or supplement [N5-F4].

These self-management strategies help maintain stable blood glucose and reduce the risk of complications [N5-F4][N3-F3].

## What blood tests and criteria are used to diagnose type 2 diabetes?

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using blood tests that measure glucose or average glucose over time. The main tests are:

- **A1C test**: Measures average blood glucose over the past 2 to 3 months. An A1C of **6.5% or higher** confirms diabetes [N2-F2].  
- **Fasting plasma glucose (FPG)**: Measures glucose after at least 8 hours of fasting. A fasting blood glucose of **126 mg/dL or higher** confirms diabetes [N2-F2].  
- **Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)**: Measures glucose before and 2 hours after drinking a sweet drink. A 2-hour blood glucose of **200 mg/dL or higher** confirms diabetes [N2-F2].  
- **Random blood glucose test**: Measures glucose at any time. A random blood glucose of **200 mg/dL or higher**, especially with symptoms of high blood sugar, may confirm diabetes [N2-F2].  

Prediabetes is the intermediate stage before diabetes and is diagnosed with:
- A1C of **5.7% to 6.4%**
- Fasting blood glucose of **100 to 125 mg/dL**
- OGTT 2-hour blood glucose of **140 to 199 mg/dL** [N2-F2].

## Common symptoms and signs that may point to the condition

Type 2 diabetes often has no clear symptoms at first, but people may notice:
- **Frequent urination** [N6-R3]
- **Excessive thirst** [N6-R5]
- **High blood glucose levels** [N6-R3]
- **High levels of ketones in the urine** [N6-R3]
- **Weight loss**, even if the person is overweight [N6-R5]
- **Blurred vision** [N6-R5]
- **Fatigue** or **weakness** [N6-R5]
- **Dry skin and mouth** [N6-R2]
- **Flushing face** or **muscle stiffness or aches** [N6-R2]

These signs are not exclusive to diabetes and can overlap with other conditions, so testing is needed for confirmation [N2-F2].

## Differences between prediabetes, diabetes, and other related conditions

- **Prediabetes**: Blood glucose levels are higher than normal but not high enough to be diagnosed as diabetes. It is a warning sign and can be reversed with lifestyle changes [N2-F2].
- **Diabetes**: Blood glucose levels are high enough to cause symptoms and meet one of the diagnostic criteria listed above [N2-F2].
- **Other related conditions**:
  - **Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)**: A severe, life-threatening complication of diabetes where the body produces high levels of ketones and blood glucose is extremely high. It is not the same as prediabetes or ordinary diabetes, and it requires urgent care [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].
  - **Hyperglycemia**: High blood glucose that may be part of diabetes, prediabetes, or other disorders [N6-R5].
  - **Hypoglycemia**: Low blood glucose, which is not the same as diabetes but can occur with insulin or certain medications [N6-R4].

The distinction matters because prediabetes is treatable, diabetes needs ongoing management, and DKA is a medical emergency [N2-F2][N6-R3].

Type 2 diabetes can damage organs and blood vessels over time, leading to complications:

- **Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)**: A severe complication where the body produces high levels of ketones and blood glucose is extremely high. DKA can develop rapidly and is a medical emergency [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

- **High blood glucose levels**
- **Ketones in the urine**
- **Blurred vision**
- **Excessive thirst or frequent urination**

## First-line and second-line treatment options including lifestyle changes

The treatment approach for type 2 diabetes is usually **lifestyle first**, followed by **medications** if needed.

### First-line treatment
- **Lifestyle changes** are the foundation of management. These include:
  - **Diet**: Eating balanced meals with appropriate carbohydrates, protein, and healthy fats [N5-F4].
  - **Exercise**: At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week, plus strength training [N5-F4].
  - **Weight loss**: Losing even a small amount of weight can improve blood glucose control [N5-F4].
- **Metformin** is the most commonly prescribed first-line medication because it is effective, safe, and generally does not cause hypoglycemia [N3-F3][N7-R3].

### Second-line and other treatment options
If metformin alone is not enough, additional medications may be added:
- **DPP-4 inhibitors** (e.g., sitagliptin, saxagliptin) help improve A1C by increasing active GLP-1 and GIP hormones [N3-F3].
- **GLP-1 receptor agonists** (e.g., dulaglutide, liraglutide, semaglutide) are injectable medications that improve glucose control and may also help with weight loss [N3-F3][N3-R2].
- **SGLT2 inhibitors** (e.g., empagliflozin, canagliflozin) lower glucose by excreting excess glucose in the urine and may reduce heart and kidney risks [N3-F3].
- **Sulfonylureas** stimulate insulin release from the pancreas, but they can cause hypoglycemia [N3-F3].
- **Thiazolidinediones (TZDs)** improve insulin sensitivity but are less commonly used today [N3-F3].

### When to consider insulin
Insulin is usually added when blood glucose is not well controlled with other medications, especially during illness, surgery, or severe stress [N3-F3].

## How different medications work and their side effects

- **Metformin**:
  - Works by reducing glucose production in the liver and improving insulin sensitivity in muscle tissue [N3-F3].
  - Common side effect: diarrhea, which often improves when taken with food [N3-F3].

- **DPP-4 inhibitors**:
  - Prevent the breakdown of GLP-1 and GIP, allowing these hormones to lower blood glucose when elevated [N3-F3].
  - Side effects are generally mild and do not usually cause weight gain or hypoglycemia [N3-F3].

- **GLP-1 receptor agonists**:
  - Act like natural GLP-1 and GIP hormones; they also reduce appetite and can promote weight loss [N3-F3][N3-R2].
  - Common side effect: nausea and vomiting, especially when starting or increasing the dose [N3-F3].

- **SGLT2 inhibitors**:
  - Block glucose reabsorption in the kidneys, causing glucose to be excreted in the urine [N3-F3].
  - Common side effects include genital yeast infections and urinary tract infections [N3-F3].

- **Sulfonylureas**:
  - Stimulate the pancreas to release more insulin [N3-F3].
  - Can cause hypoglycemia, especially in older adults or those with kidney disease [N3-F3].

## Daily self-management strategies for blood glucose monitoring and diet

A practical daily routine includes:

### Blood glucose monitoring
- Check blood glucose regularly as recommended by the healthcare provider.
- Use self-monitoring devices to track patterns and adjust treatment as needed [N5-F4].
- Check before and after exercise, as physical activity can lower blood glucose [N5-F4].

### Diet
- Eat a balanced diet with a focus on whole foods, fiber, lean protein, and healthy fats [N5-F4].
- Avoid excessive refined sugars, processed foods, and sugary drinks [N5-F4].
- Control portion sizes and manage carbohydrate intake to avoid blood glucose spikes [N5-F4].

### Lifestyle
- **Exercise regularly**: Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week, plus strength training [N5-F4].
- **Stay hydrated**: Drinking enough water helps manage blood glucose and prevents dehydration [N5-F4].
- **Manage stress**: Chronic stress can affect blood glucose and overall health [N5-F4].
- **Sleep well**: Poor sleep can worsen blood glucose control [N5-F4].

### Daily reminders
- Keep a diabetes management journal to record blood glucose readings, meals, exercise, and symptoms [N5-F4].
- Check with the healthcare provider before starting any new exercise, medication, or supplement [N5-F4].

These self-management strategies help maintain stable blood glucose and reduce the risk of complications [N5-F4][N3-F3].

- **Hyperglycemia**: Persistent high blood glucose is the main feature of the disease [N1-R1].

## What blood tests and criteria are used to diagnose type 2 diabetes?

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using blood tests that measure glucose or average glucose over time. The main tests are:

- **Fasting plasma glucose (FPG)**: Measures glucose after at least 8 hours of fasting. A fasting blood glucose of **126 mg/dL or higher** confirms diabetes [N2-F2].  
- **Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)**: Measures glucose before and 2 hours after drinking a sweet drink. A 2-hour blood glucose of **200 mg/dL or higher** confirms diabetes [N2-F2].  
- **Random blood glucose test**: Measures glucose at any time. A random blood glucose of **200 mg/dL or higher**, especially with symptoms of high blood sugar, may confirm diabetes [N2-F2].  

Prediabetes is the intermediate stage before diabetes and is diagnosed with:
- A1C of **5.7% to 6.4%**
- Fasting blood glucose of **100 to 125 mg/dL**

- **Sulfonylureas**: Stimulate the pancreas to release more insulin; can cause hypoglycemia, especially in older adults or those with kidney disease [N3-F3].

## Daily self-management strategies

A practical daily routine includes regular blood glucose monitoring, a healthy diet, and regular exercise.

### Blood glucose monitoring
- Check blood glucose regularly as recommended by your healthcare provider.
- Use self-monitoring devices to track patterns and adjust treatment as needed [N5-F4].
- Check before and after exercise, since physical activity can lower blood glucose [N5-F4].

### Diet
- Eat a balanced diet with whole foods, fiber, lean protein, and healthy fats [N5-F4].
- Avoid excessive refined sugars, processed foods, and sugary drinks [N5-F4].
- Control portion sizes and manage carbohydrate intake to avoid blood glucose spikes [N5-F4].

### Lifestyle
- **Exercise regularly**: Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week, plus strength training [N5-F4].
- **Stay hydrated**: Drinking enough water helps manage blood glucose and prevents dehydration [N5-F4].
- **Manage stress**: Chronic stress can affect blood glucose and overall health [N5-F4].
- **Sleep well**: Poor sleep can worsen blood glucose control [N5-F4].

### Daily reminders
- Keep a diabetes management journal to record blood glucose readings, meals, exercise, and symptoms [N5-F4].
- Check with your healthcare provider before starting any new exercise, medication, or supplement [N5-F4].

## What are the major complications and how they develop?

Over time, high blood sugar can damage organs and blood vessels, leading to serious complications:

- **Heart disease and stroke**: Persistent high blood sugar damages blood vessels and the heart, increasing the risk of heart attack, stroke, and cardiovascular disease [N4-R1][N4-R5].
- **Kidney disease**: Diabetes can damage the kidneys, leading to chronic kidney disease and, in severe cases, dialysis or transplant [N4-R3][N4-R4].
- **Nerve damage (neuropathy)**: High blood sugar injures nerves, especially in the feet and hands, causing pain, numbness, or weakness [N4-R3][N4-R4].
- **Eye problems**: Diabetes damages blood vessels in the retina, increasing the risk of retinopathy, cataracts, and glaucoma [N4-R4].
- **Foot problems**: Nerve damage and poor circulation can lead to ulcers, infections, and, in severe cases, amputation [N4-R3].
- **Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)**: A severe complication where the body produces high levels of ketones and blood glucose is extremely high. DKA can develop rapidly and is a medical emergency [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

These complications develop gradually because high blood sugar harms blood vessels and organs over years, especially if blood glucose is not well controlled [N4-R4][N4-R5].

## How to reduce risk of heart disease, kidney disease, and nerve damage

The best way to reduce risk is to keep blood glucose, blood pressure, and cholesterol within target ranges.

- **Control blood glucose** with medication, diet, and lifestyle changes [N3-F3].
- **Manage blood pressure**: High blood pressure worsens diabetes complications, so it should be kept below target [N4-R1][N4-R4].
- **Lower cholesterol**: Especially LDL cholesterol, to reduce heart disease risk [N4-R1][N4-R5].
- **Lose weight and keep weight stable**: Weight loss improves insulin sensitivity and reduces complications [N3-F3][N5-F4].
- **Exercise regularly**: Exercise improves blood glucose control, lowers cardiovascular risk, and improves well-being [N5-R1][N5-R3].
- **Stop smoking**: Smoking increases heart disease and other complications [N5-F4].
- **Check feet regularly**: For neuropathy, ulcers, and poor circulation [N4-R3].
- **Control other risk factors**: Such as sleep apnea, obesity, and inflammation [N4-R4].

## When to seek urgent care or specialist help

You should contact your healthcare provider immediately if you notice signs of serious complications:

- **High blood glucose levels**
- **Ketones in the urine**
- **Blurred vision**
- **Excessive thirst or frequent urination**
- **Foot pain, numbness, or sores**
- **Swelling in the legs or feet**
- **Changes in vision or eye pain** [N2-F2][N6-R3][N4-R3].

If any of these signals appear, prompt medical care is important [N2-F2][N6-R3].

## Summary for the patient

- Type 2 diabetes is a chronic condition where the body has trouble using insulin properly, leading to high blood sugar [N1-R1].
- It is diagnosed using A1C, fasting blood glucose, OGTT, or random blood glucose tests [N2-F2].
- Prediabetes is an early stage that can be reversed with lifestyle changes [N2-F2].
- Lifestyle changes and metformin are usually the first steps in treatment [N5-F4][N3-F3].
- Other medications include DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors, and sulfonylureas, each with different ways of working and side effects [N3-F3].
- Daily self-management includes blood glucose monitoring, a healthy diet, regular exercise, and stress and sleep management [N5-F4].
- Major complications include heart disease, kidney disease, nerve damage, eye problems, and DKA, which develop over time if blood glucose is not well controlled [N4-R1][N4-R5].
- If you have symptoms such as high blood glucose, ketones, blurred vision, or foot problems, seek urgent care [N2-F2][N6-R3][N4-R3].

If you want a personalized plan or have questions about your specific situation, talk with your healthcare provider.
